verdicts.why: readFieldValue dispatches 'F' to readTable (line 181) and 'A' to readArray (line 184), and both re-enter readFieldValue (lines 150 and 245), with no depth counter or nesting guard anywhere in the file; each nesting level costs ~5-6 wire bytes, so a single frame can drive tens of thousands of frames of mutual recursion.

Lines 86-89 allocate `new byte[(int)contentLength]` from a wire-supplied 32-bit length guarded only by `contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE`, and the allocation happens BEFORE `in.readFully(buffer)`, so no upstream frame-size bound can prevent a ~2GB allocation from a few bytes of input.

Same code as V02: the only check at line 87 is `< Integer.MAX_VALUE`, so a declared length of 0x7FFFFFFE allocates ~2GB at line 88 before any byte is read; the only imprecision is that readTable/readArray reach readBytes through readFieldValue -> readLongstr (line 163), not directly at lines 142/240.

Nothing is allocated in proportion to tableLength: lines 145-147 create only an empty HashMap and a TruncatedInputStream wrapper (a counter), and the loop at line 148 is driven by `tableIn.available()`, i.e. by bytes actually present, so a huge declared length allocates nothing and reads nothing extra — the claimed 'unbounded memory allocation via table length' mechanism does not exist in this code.

Whether `available()` at lines 148 and 244 is a sound EOF test depends entirely on TruncatedInputStream.available() and on which stream the callers hand to ValueReader; neither TruncatedInputStream nor any caller exists under the target path (only ValueReader.java and pom.xml), so the answer lives outside these files.

Lines 240-243 allocate only a stream wrapper and an empty ArrayList; the wire-supplied `length` is used solely as a truncation limit, never as an allocation size, and the ArrayList grows one element per value actually parsed from real bytes at line 245 — so a declared 4GB length consumes no memory by itself.
